analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals and insurers to publish negotiated prices and give consumers a cost-estimator tool.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring hospitals and insurers to disclose negotiated prices was introduced in January 2025 with zero cosponsors and has sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since, with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes hospital and health insurer price disclosure rules directly into federal law. Hospitals would have to publish their list prices, the rates they negotiated with each insurer, cash discounts, and billing codes for at least 300 common services, in a free, machine-readable format. Insurance plans would have to publish in-network and out-of-network rates, negotiated prescription drug prices, and offer a free online tool so patients can see what a service will actually cost them before they get the bill. Violating hospitals could face a civil penalty of up to $300 per day.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and anyone paying for health care. Someone getting a knee MRI or a scheduled surgery could look up what their insurer actually pays at different hospitals and what they would owe out of pocket before committing. Uninsured patients would see discounted cash prices that many hospitals keep off their websites. Employers who buy health plans for workers would also get visibility into the rates their money covers.

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals must publish, in plain language and free of charge, their gross charges, the specific rates negotiated with each named insurer, discounted cash prices, and billing codes, for at least 300 shoppable services [S3].

Hospitals would be deemed compliant if they maintain a free internet-based price estimator tool that shows consumers what they would actually pay, searchable by service, billing code, and insurer [S3].

Insurance plans must disclose in-network rates, out-of-network allowed amounts, and negotiated prescription drug rates including historical net prices after rebates, and must provide a free self-service tool with real-time cost-sharing estimates [S3].
Hospitals that fail to comply after a corrective action plan face a civil monetary penalty of up to $300 per day while the violation continues [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals and health insurers bear the costs of building, maintaining, and updating the price publications and consumer tools, and they lose the pricing secrecy that comes from keeping negotiated rates confidential. PBMs and insurers would have to reveal drug prices net of rebates. Compliance costs are likely passed to consumers in some form through premiums and charges.

drawbacks.text: The penalty for a hospital that refuses to publish its prices is capped at $300 per day, which for a large hospital system is a rounding error and gives regulators little leverage against a determined violator [S3].

Publishing rates does not by itself lower prices; many consumers will never use the data, and researchers have found the already-existing version of these disclosure rules has had limited effect on what patients actually pay. The bill's main practical change is making permanent rules that already exist administratively.

Hospitals and insurers would face real compliance costs building and maintaining machine-readable price files and consumer-facing estimate tools, and some of that cost would likely show up in premiums or charges [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is real but indirect: knowing prices does not guarantee a better deal, and the disclosure rules it codifies largely already exist under federal regulations, so the bill's incremental effect is modest. Its biggest value is durability, putting the rules in statute so they cannot be quietly rescinded. The weak $300-a-day penalty undercuts enforcement, which is the bill's most serious design flaw. On balance it is a low-cost, pro-consumer bill that falls well short of what the underlying problem demands.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in January 2025 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has not moved since.

narrative.text: Rep. Warren Davidson introduced the bill in the House on January 9, 2025 [S1].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is where health pricing legislation sits before any floor consideration [S5].
The bill has no cosponsors, so no other member has formally signed on [S4].
As of the latest action record, the committee has taken no further step, with no hearing, markup, or floor vote [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, hospitals and insurers keep the pricing status quo, since the bill has produced no action and nothing has changed for patients yet.

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan pattern has formed yet.

industries.note: Hospitals would have to publish their negotiated rates with each insurer, cash discounts, and billing codes for at least 300 services, ending the information advantage they get from opaque pricing. Hospital groups fought the existing version of this rule in court, and a statute would take away the option of a friendlier administration quietly dropping it.

Plans would have to publish in-network and out-of-network rates and provide a free cost-estimator tool, and the requirement would apply to employer group plans as well as marketplace plans. Insurers lose the negotiating secrecy that lets them charge different rates to different buyers.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug pricing intermediaries
industries.note: Insurers would have to publish negotiated drug rates and historical net prices net of rebates and fees, which would expose how much of a drug's list price is captured by intermediaries. The disclosure requirement stops short of forcing any change in how those rebates are shared.

analysis.trajectory: With no cosponsors and no committee action for months, the bill faces long odds. Price transparency codification has drawn occasional interest from both parties, so it could pick up cosponsors if leadership takes it up, but a bill sitting untouched in Energy and Commerce typically dies quietly when the Congress ends.
